book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

chapters.file: ch31 - 29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself.md
chapters.relation: Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.

chapters.file: ch32 - 30. The Boys as Philosophy Superheroes, Fascism, and the American Right.md
chapters.relation: Johnson treats The Boys as an argument from analogy that MAGA Trumpism is fascist, walking through how the show equates Homelander and Vought with the Nazi supe Stormfront and with Trump: the Big Lie, gaslighting, fearmongering, over-policing, conspiracy theories (QAnon as rebranded blood libel), cults of personality, projection, and loyal propaganda outlets. Drawing on Wittgenstein's notion of family resemblance, he argues 'fascism' has no necessary-and-sufficient definition but a cluster of shared traits, and compiling scholars' checklists shows MAGA belongs to the fascist family. Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism supplies the 'alternative universe' of nonfacts and the leader who is 'always right,' and he invokes the banality of evil and totalitarian fiction to gauge the analogy's strength.

chapters.file: ch34 - 31. Inception as Philosophy Choose Your Dreams or Seek Reality.md
chapters.relation: Johnson uses Nolan's Inception—Cobb's dream-heists, the ambiguous spinning top, and the case that the whole film may be a dream—to test the moral Todd McGowan draws from it: that since we can't be sure what is real, we should abandon the quest for reality and choose the dream (his object of desire, his children) as Cobb does at the end. He evaluates six defenses of that moral, rejecting Descartes' skeptical dream/evil-demon problem (answered by abduction and by Plato's cave and Nozick's experience machine showing true belief is valuable), Baudrillard's denial of reality, Locke/Kant on the unknowable noumenal world, and Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Pascal's Wager, before softening it with Hume's return from skepticism to backgammon: entertain the doubt, then walk away when your children walk in.

chapters.file: ch35 - 32. Okja as Philosophy Why Animals Matter.md
chapters.relation: Jensen frames Okja around three views of the super-pig Okja's moral status: Mirando treats her as mere property, the Animal Liberation Front as a symbol to be sacrificed for the cause, and the girl Mija as a friend and person. He dismantles Mirando's 'human exceptionalism'—amoralism, Aquinas's natural-law teleology, the Kantian persons-only view, and Descartes' claim that animals are unfeeling automata—then develops the ALF's liberation through Singer's equal consideration of interests, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and speciesism as prejudice, weighing consequentialist (utilitarian) against deontological (rights, Regan) foundations. He closes with hierarchical moral status and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many,' arguing Mija's love for Okja shows that at some point relationship matters more than moral calculation.

chapters.file: ch36 - 33. 2001 as Philosophy A Technological Odyssey.md
chapters.relation: Abrams argues that Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey dramatizes Henri Bergson's Creative Evolution and Two Sources of Morality and Religion better than Nietzsche's Zarathustra: the monolith turning Moonwatcher's bone into a tool makes humanity Homo faber, and the match-cut from bone to satellite traces one technological odyssey toward species self-transformation. He reads the HAL 9000's murderous breakdown through Turing's imitation game—Hal passes the Turing Test and inverts it by testing Frank at chess and probing Dave—and casts Dave as a new Odysseus dousing HAL the Cyclops. The star child is Bergson's vision of the universe as 'a machine for making gods,' the Nietzschean overman realized through Bergsonian creative and technological evolution, with Aristotle's mimesis grounding the film's account of imitation and its own cinematic self-reflection.

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief
holes.what: W.K. Clifford's principle that it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence, since beliefs guide action and endanger others.
holes.why: Chapter 31's central positive argument—that people must not accept religious views without good grounds—rests wholly on Clifford's 'Ethics of Belief,' which recurs and is also load-bearing in chapter 34, and no existing philosopher or concept slug covers Clifford.

holes.name: Fascism
holes.what: A family of ultranationalist, authoritarian political ideologies exalting a leader-cult, in-group myth, and forcible suppression of opposition, defined by family resemblance rather than necessary-and-sufficient conditions.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is entirely an argument that MAGA Trumpism is fascist and analyzes fascism's defining traits at length; the taxonomy has arendt-totalitarianism but no slug for fascism itself, which is the chapter's core concept.
